# Tally × Neatlogs: audit and implementation plan

**Audited:** 11 October 2026  
**Repository:** `Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack`, branch `codex/first-user-integrations`  
**Scope:** Read-only source audit, current Neatlogs documentation/API contract, and the neatHack requirements. No source changes, test runs, issue creation, PRs, or remote writes were made.

## Executive assessment

There is real Neatlogs integration code in Tally, but it is not yet a working, end-to-end observability loop on this machine. The code has two distinct ideas:

1. Tally emits its own traces for sizing/routing/escalation decisions and attempt history.
2. Neatlogs’ Codex hooks are intended to capture the actual coding-agent turn: model phases, tool calls, failures, and subagent work.

The second is the evidence judges and Tally users need most. On the audited host, the project’s local SDK packages exist, but no Neatlogs credentials/configuration or Codex hooks are installed. So a live Tally run here is not currently set up to send Tally traces or capture the AO-launched Codex worker.

Even when configured, the application-side traces are shallow: several separate decision traces, a separate nearly empty history trace per attempt, and one trace per five-second ceiling poll. They do not yet form a coherent task/run trace that shows the whole path from issue intake through model/tool work, verification, escalation, and PR. The dashboard stores and displays trace IDs but the run code leaves their URL fields null. The only intended decision feedback from remote Neatlogs data is aggregate pass-rate/cost history; that read path currently requests 100 traces even though the current API caps trace pages at 50, then silently falls back to local history.

The blunt assessment: **Tally has built a Neatlogs transport and some trace hooks, but has not yet turned Neatlogs into a product capability.** The next work should first unblock the first-user setup, then capture one complete, correlated task attempt, then use the trace to explain and measure a before/after improvement.

## What is the source of truth today?

| Data | Current authority | Neatlogs’ role |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub backlog and published PR | GitHub | Not authoritative |
| Run/task status, verification result, attempt ledger, recorded per-attempt spend estimate | Tally’s local `.tally/runs/<run-id>/run.json` and `ledger.json` | Evidence/correlation only |
| Live budget/spend when cfo.ai is enabled | cfo.ai, with Tally’s local integer-nanos ledger and fallback CSV | Not authoritative |
| Local routing history | `.tally/history.json` beside the Tally config | Persistent local fallback and writer |
| Shared routing history, when a read token and project ID are configured | A remote aggregate of recent Neatlogs trace records, preferred over local history when it returns observations | Can affect which tier Tally selects; currently brittle and likely falling back due to an API page-size mismatch |
| Worker prompts, tool calls, model phases, and subagent work | Codex hook events, if the Neatlogs Codex hook is installed in the environment that runs AO workers | Neatlogs stores and presents the actual worker trace |
| Entire checkpoints and handoff context | Entire IDs/metadata plus local ledger | Separate evidence; not a Neatlogs source of truth |

The repo README describes the local ledger and verification as persisted run evidence, and says cfo.ai is the live accounting authority when enabled. `engine/real.ts` writes the run and ledger files; `engine/output.ts` mirrors the latest run. `adapters/history-file.ts` persists the local pass-rate/cost cells.

Neatlogs has two credentials with different jobs. `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` is used to send traces. `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` plus `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` is optional read access for the Public API and remote history/readback. Current Neatlogs docs explicitly say SDK ingest credentials do not grant Public API reads; the API uses project-bound service-account/OAuth credentials and scoped access ([authentication and scopes](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/authentication)).

## What code uses Neatlogs now?

### 1. Tally’s own SDK traces

`adapters/neatlogs.ts` lazily imports the `neatlogs` TypeScript SDK and initializes it as workflow `tally-cfo-agent`, tagged `tally` and `cfo-agent`. Its generic `TracePort.span()` always opens a `CHAIN` trace, passes the same small attribute map as both input and attributes, runs a callback, and tries to extract the trace ID from the active W3C carrier. Export failures are intended not to execute application work twice or fail the run.

The `TracePort` is passed through `agent/trace.ts` into:

- `agent/sizer.ts`: `tally.size`
- `agent/router.ts`: `tally.route`
- `agent/baseline.ts`: `tally.baseline.route`
- `agent/escalation.ts`: `tally.escalate`
- `agent/watcher.ts`: `tally.ceiling.poll`

Those are useful starting points. Neatlogs’ TypeScript SDK supports nested spans, explicit trace roots, custom attributes, sessions, and flush/shutdown; a trace is most useful when the actual workflow tree is represented, not merely when an SDK call succeeds ([TypeScript SDK](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript), [trace concepts](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/traces)).

### 2. Attempt-history traces and routing feedback

After an attempt finishes, `engine/real.ts:recordHistory()` first writes the outcome to the configured history writer. For a real run with Neatlogs enabled, it then emits an empty callback named like `tally.history.record size=... tier=... result=... cost_nanos=...` with attempt attributes. The trace name itself encodes the outcome. Dry runs do not emit this trace.

When optional read access is present, `NeatlogsPriceHistory.lookup()` lists traces for `tally-cfo-agent`, parses observations from the trace name (and sometimes spans), averages pass rate/cost by task size and tier, and uses that remote aggregate if any matching observations exist. Otherwise it falls back to `.tally/history.json`. `record()` still writes to the local fallback; the SDK trace is the path that places the remote observation in Neatlogs.

There is a high-confidence contract mismatch here: `NeatlogsPriceHistory` defaults to `limit=100`, but the current Public API contract sets `GET /api/v1/public/traces` to a maximum page size of 50. The code catches a failed request and silently returns local history, so a user can believe shared Neatlogs history is influencing routing when it is not. The current API also uses cursor pagination; Tally does not follow cursors in this adapter. This is verifiable from the live contract ([List traces](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/endpoints/traces/get_api_v1_public_traces), [pagination](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination)).

The other weakness is data quality: remote history is grouped only by `(size, tier name)`. It does not distinguish model/version, harness, route-policy version, repository/task family, or price-schedule version. Old outcomes can therefore influence a new model or configuration. It has no freshness or minimum-sample provenance surfaced to the planner.

### 3. Actual Codex worker traces

The repo depends on `@neatlogs/codex` and has `NeatlogsWorkerSpoolAdapter` and `NeatlogsWorkerTraceReader`:

- The Codex hook writes OTLP spans to a local spool.
- After an AO worker finishes, Tally drains selected batches outside the worker sandbox.
- Tally then optionally queries the Public API to verify a readable worker trace and saves its ID in the ledger.
- `engine/trace-recovery.ts` can retry a failed worker-trace drain/readback for a finished run.

This is the strongest sponsor-product fit. The current Codex integration documents one trace per main-thread user prompt, including model phases, tool calls, and subagent work, and documents a local/project setup alternative to global setup ([Codex Hooks](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/codex)).

However, the hook has to be installed where the AO-launched Codex process actually runs. On the audited host, the workspace has `neatlogs@1.1.28` and `@neatlogs/codex@0.1.1` (both the current registry versions observed on 11 October), but the hook status reported `hooksFileExists: false` and `apiKeyConfigured: false`; `~/.codex/hooks.json`, `~/.config/neatlogs/config.json`, and `~/.tally/.env` were absent. The Codex hook is therefore **not configured here**, despite the dependency being installed in the project. If AO runs Codex in another environment, inspect/configure that worker host instead.

The current worker readback also relies on string matching: `NeatlogsWorkerTraceReader` requires the trace’s session ID to equal the Entire native session ID and looks for `Tally run ..., task ..., attempt ...` inside `workflowName`/`traceName`. The Codex hook currently derives workflow name from the prompt and truncates it to 80 characters. Tally puts a correlation sentence in the prompt, but a durable explicit attribute would be safer than relying on a display-name convention. The current code/tests assume this mapping; a real worker trace from this host has not been available to verify it.

### 4. Status and dashboard

The project has a known first-user-flow bug in open issue [#89: Skip disabled neatlogs in tally doctor](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/89), found while working toward [#88: Validate the first-user Tally flow](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/88). `engine/doctor.ts` reports the Neatlogs key as missing even when Neatlogs is disabled; the CLI treats a missing line as failure. That makes an optional sponsor integration block unrelated first-time setup.

Trace IDs are represented separately in the ledger as a decision trace ID and a worker trace ID, which is good. But the code sets `traceUrl` and `workerTraceUrl` to `null`, and `dashboard/app.js` falls back to copyable IDs instead of opening the corresponding Neatlogs trace. The integration status is also too coarse to tell these states apart: SDK initialized, Tally trace exported, worker hook captured, worker batch drained, and worker trace read back.

## How badly are we using Neatlogs?

1. **The live integration is not configured on this host.** There is no key/config or hook file, so there is no evidence of current application or worker traces reaching Neatlogs from here.
2. **The Tally SDK traces are fragments, not an end-to-end run.** Each generic `span()` creates a top-level `CHAIN` trace when there is no common parent. A run’s sizing/routing/escalation/verification/PR work cannot be followed as one coherent tree.
3. **The worker trace—the most valuable data—is optional and not yet demonstrated.** The spool and readback path exist, but the hooks are not installed here and correlation depends on session/name assumptions.
4. **The watcher is over-instrumented.** `CeilingWatcher.poll()` is traced each time it runs (every five seconds during a live attempt). This can create a stream of low-value one-operation traces while still omitting a clean attempt summary. Record the final usage and the ceiling-crossing event on the attempt trace instead.
5. **The history trace is acting like a database row encoded in a trace name.** It has no children and no agent/model/tool activity. It is a workaround, not meaningful observability.
6. **Remote history may never be read.** `limit=100` violates the current endpoint’s maximum of 50; the catch-all fallback hides the failure. Even corrected, missing cursors, repeated uncached API calls, and thin metadata make the result fragile.
7. **The remote feedback is too broad to safely route on.** `(size, tier name)` is insufficient when model/harness/pricing/policy changes; no age/minimum-sample guard or source is shown to users.
8. **No trace-to-product loop exists yet.** Worker trace IDs are not used by sizing, escalation, verification, dashboard links, detection rules, or evaluations. The only remote feedback loop is the limited price-history aggregate.
9. **The UI makes the evidence hard to inspect.** IDs can be copied, but the run dashboard does not provide direct links to the decision and worker traces.
10. **The setup blast radius is unnecessarily broad by default.** Tally asks whether to install global Claude Code and Codex hooks, which traces every session on the machine. Neatlogs supports project-scoped Codex setup; prefer that when it works with AO worktrees, and make global setup an explicit opt-in with an explanation. Since hooks can capture prompts and tool inputs/outputs, keep data scope and local masking visible in the choice. Neatlogs distinguishes local SDK masking from server-side redaction; server settings alone do not protect data before it leaves the process ([PII Redaction](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/pii-redaction)).

## Target integration design

Keep Tally’s local run state/ledger authoritative for task outcome and spend accounting. Use Neatlogs as the inspectable trace/evaluation layer around an attempt, and use remote history only as a bounded, versioned planning signal.

### Trace shape

For the first useful version, make one Tally-owned root trace per task, with `sessionId = runId` so tasks from one multi-task run group together. Use a `WORKFLOW` root and nest spans underneath it:

```text
tally.task (WORKFLOW; sessionId=runId)
├── intake / impact (TOOL or RETRIEVER)
├── size and route (CHAIN)
├── attempt 1 (TOOL: ao worker lifecycle)
│   ├── Codex worker trace (linked by stable run/task/attempt IDs)
│   ├── budget checks (GUARDRAIL; summarize, do not emit every poll)
│   ├── checkpoint / handoff (TOOL)
│   └── verify (GUARDRAIL)
├── escalation decision (CHAIN)
├── attempt 2 (if present)
└── publish PR and reconcile spend (TOOL)
```

The actual Codex trace should retain the rich model/tool/subagent spans supplied by the official hook package. Link it to the Tally-owned task trace with stable `tally.run_id`, `tally.task_id`, and `tally.attempt` attributes, plus the saved worker trace ID. Do not make a prompt prefix or trace display name the permanent join key. True parent-child continuity across the AO process boundary can be a later spike using Neatlogs’ W3C `injectTraceContext`/`extractTraceContext`, but only if AO can pass that context safely and the hook can consume it; linked traces are a valid first milestone.

### Recommended attributes

Keep attributes small, typed, and useful for filtering. Do not attach the whole GitHub issue, repository files, patch, or command output to the Tally-owned spans by default.

- Run: `tally.run_id`, `tally.mode`, `tally.backlog_source`, `tally.budget_source`, `tally.policy_version`.
- Task: `tally.task_id`, `tally.task_size`, `tally.size_source`, `tally.impact_files_count`, `tally.impact_dependents`, `tally.tests_present`.
- Route: chosen tier/model/harness, estimated pass rate, observed sample count, expected cost, ceiling, and whether the source was local history, remote history, or prior.
- Attempt: attempt number, model/tier, AO status, result category, tokens, estimated cost, cost source, duration, escalation outcome, verifier pass/fail, changed-file count, PR-created boolean.
- Worker link: native session ID and verified worker trace ID; avoid logging credentials or raw session transcripts in Tally metadata.

The coding-agent hook intentionally captures richer prompt/tool evidence; make that consent explicit and verify its actual host. Neatlogs documents that the hook emits model/tool/session context and redacts common secret-bearing fields, but its presence is not a reason to send private repository content indiscriminately ([Codex Hooks](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/codex), [PII Redaction](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/pii-redaction)).

## Action plan, in order

### P0 — Make first-user setup honest and unblocked

1. Address existing issue #89: when `integrations.neatlogs` is false, `tally doctor` should report `off` (or omit the check) and not fail. Require a Neatlogs key only when the user enabled Neatlogs.
2. Split Neatlogs status into distinct checks: write key present/probe passed; SDK available; Codex hook installed on the AO worker host; worker spool drained; Public API readback verified. Do not report “connected” as proof that the application emitted a trace.
3. Keep the ingest key and service-account read token separate in prompts and status. Public API read access is optional; lack of it must not block trace ingestion.
4. Prefer project-scoped Codex hooks where AO’s worker worktrees load them. If they do not, explain that global installation covers every local session and ask for that choice explicitly.
5. Verify the installed SDK’s local Doctor and a synthetic authenticated probe according to the current Doctor docs. Label this as pipeline/credential verification only: Neatlogs states that a synthetic probe does not prove the user’s application ran or produced a trace ([SDK Doctor](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/doctor)).

**P0 acceptance:** With Neatlogs off and no Neatlogs secrets, `tally doctor` and the guided first-user flow succeed. With Neatlogs on, the UI identifies separately whether Tally telemetry and worker tracing are configured, without printing secrets or claiming a real trace before one is read back.

### P1 — Capture one useful task trace

1. Refactor the generic trace port so a task-level `WORKFLOW` root can stay active while sizer/router/escalation/verifier spans run beneath it. Use SDK-documented span kinds rather than forcing every operation through the same `CHAIN` wrapper.
2. Wrap the worker lifecycle and verifier/publisher calls with Tally-owned spans. Record start/wait/final usage/stop/failure/verification outcomes and a concise error category. Preserve the current rule that telemetry failure never reruns work or converts a successful task into failure.
3. Remove per-poll trace creation. Keep the ceiling watcher’s safety behavior, but emit a single attempt summary plus a budget-stop event/attributes.
4. Give worker traces explicit correlation attributes or a supported metadata bridge. Verify the relationship among AO session ID, Codex `session_id`, and Entire `entireSessionId`; do not equate them without observing a real trace.
5. Populate trace URLs after successful readback and make both decision/worker evidence clickable from the run dashboard. Keep the ID available as fallback.

**P1 acceptance:** One real, harmless test task produces a Tally task trace with route, attempt, verification, and result spans; a separately captured Codex trace contains its LLM/tool work and matches the same run/task/attempt; the local ledger outcome agrees with both; the dashboard opens both traces. Export failure leaves the local ledger correct and visible.

### P2 — Make remote history correct before it can influence routing

1. Change the list request to a legal page size (at most 50) and implement bounded cursor pagination using the opaque `data.page.nextCursor` exactly as returned. Set a hard page/trace ceiling.
2. Cache one remote history snapshot for the duration of a run instead of re-fetching the same trace list for every size/tier lookup. Batch or bound per-trace span reads and handle 401/403/429/5xx distinctly.
3. Store outcome fields as structured attributes rather than encoding the main record in `traceName`. Version the record schema and include model, harness, pricing/policy version, task size, result, cost, and timestamp.
4. Do not let remote history override local observations unless it is fresh, has a minimum sample count, and matches the current model/harness/policy identity. Show the source, age, and observation count in `tally run --plan` and the decision trace. Keep local `.tally/history.json` as the offline fallback and the local audit record.
5. If reliable shared history is not achievable within the hackathon, keep it out of routing and use Neatlogs for trace inspection and before/after evaluation instead. A narrower truthful integration is better than silently calling stale/incompatible history “connected.”

**P2 acceptance:** Contract-shaped fixtures prove the API request never exceeds 50, cursor pages are read up to a configured ceiling, remote failures are observable and fall back safely, and a plan clearly reports which history source actually informed a route.

### P3 — Use Neatlogs to improve the agent, not just retain telemetry

1. In the Neatlogs project, create a saved view/filter for Tally task traces and detections for useful anomalies: budget ceiling crossed, failed verification, repeated tool failure, unusually high cost/latency, and worker trace missing. Current detections support rules on span content and numeric/boolean attributes ([Detections](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/detections)).
2. Review one failed or escalated worker trace in Investigate: ask which step failed, what the agent saw, what tool response caused the failure, and whether the retry used the prior work. Keep the conclusions tied to linked evidence ([Investigate](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/ai-search)).
3. Add a small human/AI evaluation rubric for coding tasks: requirement coverage, test result, scope discipline, correct recovery/escalation, and cost. Score actual task traces rather than synthetic probe traces. Neatlogs’ evaluation workflow can collect structured judgments and aggregate them ([Evals](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/evals/human-evaluators)).
4. Use trace findings to make one concrete agent improvement—such as a better route threshold, handoff instruction, or verification recovery—and compare the matched before/after run evidence.

## How to measure “how much better”

No honest percentage can be promised before a matched benchmark. Instrumentation itself improves debuggability and judge-verifiable evidence; it does not automatically make the coding agent more accurate or cheaper. Measure the product change with the same issue set, base commit, model choices, verifier, and budget conditions:

- task pass rate;
- cost per passed task and total cost;
- median time to verified completion;
- first-attempt pass rate;
- escalation rate and recovery rate after first-attempt failure;
- percentage of real attempts with both a Tally trace and a worker trace;
- percentage of attempts whose trace result agrees with the local ledger.

Use `tally run --baseline --only <task>` and `tally run --only <task>` on the same isolated target/commit, recording each result. The existing `tally experiment` supports simulated comparisons, but the README says real experiment execution is currently gated; dry-run telemetry is also intentionally not exported. Do not present simulation as proof of live Neatlogs or agent improvement.

For a tiny hackathon benchmark, one matched issue before/after is acceptable as a concrete demo, but describe it as one example. If time permits, repeat several representative tasks and show a table with the numerator/denominator and exact spend. Neatlogs traces should let a judge inspect *why* the outcome changed, not just see a claimed percentage.

The official neatHack page currently says all projects must use neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai with clear roles; it asks teams to trace runs and compare before/after; its evidence examples include trace links/screenshots, Entire checkpoints/graph, a cfo.ai business plan, and a failure-recovery run. The page calls for a public code repository and a demo of three minutes or less, with all three products explicitly covered ([official neatHack requirements and judging](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)).

For Tally, present the sponsor roles as:

- **Neatlogs:** the evidence layer for a coding-agent task—what the worker was asked, model/tool steps, where it failed, cost/latency, what changed on retry, and how verification ended.
- **Entire:** code graph/checkpoint context used to size work and continue a failed attempt.
- **cfo.ai:** the business plan/unit economics and, where configured, the budget/spend authority.

Before recording the demo, collect:

- one working worker trace and one Tally task trace, both linked from the run;
- one matched before/after task with exact cost/result/latency numbers;
- one real recovery/escalation trace showing the next action after a failure;
- an Entire graph/checkpoint artifact and cfo.ai pricing/cost/revenue/runway plan;

It also says planning can happen ahead of time but code must be written during the event. Confirm the final cutoff and eligibility against the live event page/Discord before submission; this audit does not certify that the repository history meets that rule.

When implementation is authorized, add focused tests and then verify a real application trace (the audit itself did not run tests):

- Doctor: disabled integration is `off`; enabled-but-missing key is actionable; enabled key is not called connected until the agreed probe succeeds.

### Try the demo first

### How a real run works

In your target repo, Tally finds open GitHub issues with the label you configure, estimates task size, selects a model tier, and applies a per-task spending ceiling. It runs the coding agent, checks the configured test command, records the attempt and evidence, then can push a branch and open a PR for review.

For your first real run:

1. Put the `tally` label on just the one issue you want to try, and make sure the repo has a test command that passes.
2. Run `tally init --dry-run` to preview setup. `tally init` asks before applying its proposed repo and runner configuration.
3. Run `tally doctor` to see which prerequisites are ready.
4. Run `tally run --plan` to check the tasks and routing without starting workers or spending.
5. When the plan looks right, run `tally run`. This uses your agent account and may push a branch and open a PR.

The default runner is Agent Orchestrator (AO), which must be installed and running. The alternative is the direct runner, configured with `runner: direct`, which launches Codex or Claude Code itself. Either way, you need GitHub CLI access to the repo and an authenticated coding-agent account. If the RPM you installed is AO, `tally doctor` should tell you whether it’s ready.

### How the integrations fit

- **Entire** can supply repository graph and checkpoint context for sizing and handoffs.
- **Neatlogs** records worker traces and checks whether trace delivery can be read back. The current design uses it for observability and run evidence.
- **cfo.ai** can provide the monthly budget and spend source; `tally login cfoai` connects it.

Each integration is optional and defaults to off in `tally init`. The demo’s `--live` option still uses simulated workers; it only probes read-only integrations.

All are open:

## Entire: what’s online now

The checkpoints are **not only local**. The test repo’s `entire status` showed checkpoints syncing to `origin`, and `git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'` returned all six checkpoint refs on the private GitHub repo. That is why `entire checkpoint explain <id>` works locally.

They are **not yet in your Entire Web repository list**. I checked the account logged in as `github:adot-7`: it lists an unrelated `test-repo`, but `entire repo view /gh/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011` found no matching repository, and `entire repo mirror list --available --owner adot-7` returned no GitHub candidates.

To connect it:

1. Install/authorize the [Entire GitHub App](https://entire.io/blog/an-entirely-new-git-hosting-network) for the private test repo. The repo owner or an organization admin needs to grant access.
2. Recheck with `entire repo mirror list --available --owner adot-7`. The test repo should appear once access is granted.
3. Run `entire repo mirror add` and select the repo and region.
4. Verify with `entire repo view /gh/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011 --json`, then find the sessions in Entire Web.

After the repo is visible there, you can share **individual sessions** by setting the selected sessions to Public and copying their links; Entire documents public sharing for sessions from private repos. Review the session contents before sharing, since a session includes agent context. [Entire’s session-sharing guide](https://entire.io/blog/entire-dispatch-0x000d) describes this flow.

The relevant Tally code also reflects the distinction: [Entire onboarding](/home/adot/projects/agentProjects/neatlogs-hack/neatlogs-hack/onboarding/entire.ts) configures local capture and hooks, while [the publisher](/home/adot/projects/agentProjects/neatlogs-hack/neatlogs-hack/adapters/publisher.ts) pushes checkpoint refs to Git remotes. **cfo.ai:** The dedicated `Tally E2E` scenario is in the **Included Whippet** workspace. The budget was $5; verified spend was **$1.07277288**, leaving **$3.92722712**. The dedicated [budget ledger](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED) and [spend detail table](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED) are there.

content.text:
Now Neatlogs has two roles in Tally: it shows what happened during a run, and it can supply past results to help choose a model tier for future tasks.

1. **During a real run, Tally sends traces** for routing decisions and escalations. After an attempt, it also sends a structured history record with the task size, tier, result, and cost. Worker traces are drained and checked separately. These let you inspect the run and its decisions in Neatlogs.

2. **On later runs, Tally can read those history records back.** It groups them by task size and tier, then calculates attempt count, pass rate, and average cost. The router uses enough history to estimate whether starting on a cheaper tier is likely to cost less than going straight to the strongest tier. It requires at least two observations by default; with less data, it uses the configured prior instead. The route trace records the decision and its reason.

The history adapter also saves each outcome locally, so Tally can fall back to `.tally/history.json` if Neatlogs has no matching records or the remote read fails. The merged pagination fix lets it read beyond the first 50 traces, and the other merged fix makes `tally run --plan` use the same configured history source as a run. The plan output reports whether its history came from remote Neatlogs, the local fallback, or nowhere.

The important distinction: **Tally uses specific structured attempt records for routing; it doesn’t interpret arbitrary worker-trace contents to decide what model to use.** For this to work remotely, `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` enables trace sending, while `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` and `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` enable history reads. A successful Neatlogs integration status and a `remote Neatlogs` plan history source are useful evidence to show in a demo.

Yes—Tally **does use Neatlogs trace data to inform routing**. My last paragraph was meant to distinguish *which* traces it uses, but I made that distinction sound like it wasn’t using them.

Tally records structured attempt traces: task size, tier, pass/fail result, and cost. Future routing groups those records by size and tier. Once a group has at least two observations by default, Tally can use its pass rate and the strongest tier’s observed average cost to estimate whether trying a cheaper tier first makes sense. With thinner history, it falls back to configured priors. It doesn’t analyze every detail of the worker’s session trace, and more data gives it better estimates to work with—it doesn’t guarantee every run makes routing more accurate.

**Next issue: #122.** I opened [PR #129](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/129). Since Codex’s model catalog can be bundled rather than an account-access check, Tally now labels configured model access **unverified** in `tally doctor`. If a harness rejects a model, Tally preserves the error and reports the tier, model, and a fix rather than retrying the same model. ([OpenAI docs](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source/codex-app-server); [Claude Code CLI reference](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/cli-usage).) The no-spend limitation is an inference from those documented CLI capabilities.

The full suite passed: **697 tests**, typecheck, and build. GitHub’s release check passed; the PR is open and mergeable. I kept the work in an isolated worktree.

Your X draft has a strong story. I’d make two claims more precise: say the checkpoints preserve *session context* rather than promising the complete context, and describe Neatlogs as using structured attempt history rather than every trace. Also, if you created the cfo.ai tables manually, say Tally connected to and used them.

### Suggested thread

**1/** Update #2 on Tally: our CFO for AI spend.

We pointed Tally at a demo repo with six issues. @EntireHQ’s repo graph helped estimate task scope, and Tally routed each task across low-cost, mid-tier, and top-tier models.

**2/** The bit I love about Entire: checkpoints link commits back to the agent session context behind them. A PR shows the code; a checkpoint helps recover how the change came about. That context is easy to lose when an agent session ends.

**3/** We connected Tally to a dedicated @arithecfo scenario and verified its budget and spend tables. Tally reads the budget and writes tracked spend there. The Ari-in-Slack angle is compelling too: ask about spend and model scenarios without digging through logs.

**4/** @neatlogs traces feed a routing feedback loop. Tally records attempt outcomes and cost, then can use that history to inform future model choices when there are enough observations for a task-size/tier pair. With thin history, it falls back to its priors. We’re excited to test how those estimates improve as evidence builds.
